c.text: In 2006 there was an explosion in space that a NASA satellite caught for 102 seconds
It released more energy than our Sun gives off in its whole life
The world's biggest telescopes looked there at once
Then some scientists named something strange, a white hole, the exact opposite of a black hole
But do white holes really exist?

c.text: When a very big star runs out of fuel, it starts to fall inward under its own weight
and is squeezed so much that not even light can escape its gravity
That is a black hole, ringed by a boundary called the event horizon; past it, nothing comes back
In 1915 Einstein wrote the equations of gravity, and black holes came out of those very equations
but they hid something strange
These equations work exactly the same with time running forward or backward
Run a cricket replay backwards and the ball leaves the keeper's gloves and goes straight back to the bowler's hand
and to physics, both videos look perfectly right

c.at: इसी तरह black hole का replay
c.text: Run a black hole's replay backwards the same way and you get a white hole
a boundary from which light and matter only come out, and nothing can go in
In 1960, Martin Kruskal and George Szekeres drew the full mathematical map of a black hole's spacetime
and this second part turned up hidden in the equations
Maths allowed the white hole, yet most scientists refused to accept it

c.text: Their first doubt was about the direction of time
because milk boils over in the kitchen, but spilt milk never climbs back into the pot by itself
In nature things spread out; they never gather back by themselves
while a white hole does exactly that reverse, which we have never seen happen
Still, in 1964 the Russian scientist Igor Novikov said white holes could exist
but ten years later Douglas Eardley showed a big problem with it
Nothing can enter a white hole, but its gravity piles dust and radiation up just outside its boundary
By Eardley's account this piled-up matter grows so heavy that the whole white hole collapses into a black hole
So even if one formed, it would not last
The same year, 1974, Jayant Narlikar and his team at TIFR in Mumbai took a different angle
and wrote in the famous journal Nature that white holes could be behind the fastest radiation in space
For them it was a big clue to the biggest explosions in space, but for years nobody caught such a blast
Then in 2006 the Swift satellite saw that strange flash

c.text: Sometimes a very bright flash of gamma rays comes from space; it is called a gamma ray burst, and there are two kinds
Short ones last under two seconds and come from two dead stars colliding
while long ones come from a big star dying, and a supernova's light always follows

c.at: दो हज़ार छह का वो धमाका
c.text: The 2006 blast lasted 102 seconds, a long one, but no supernova followed
Scientists called it a hybrid, because it fit no category
In 2011 Alon Retter and Shlomo Heller suggested it was perhaps a white hole
which, like a Diwali anaar, threw out all its matter in one burst and was gone
They called it a Small Bang, but the story twisted when scientists later re-checked the burst's old light
and found signs of a kilonova
A kilonova is the faint light after two dead stars, neutron stars, collide, so most astronomers think it was a neutron star crash, not a white hole
There is no firm proof, but the white hole idea came back by another road

c.text: Now the very centre of a black hole, where Einstein's equations say all matter is crushed into a tiny point and density becomes infinite
But where a number becomes infinite, physics fails: at such tiny scales quantum physics rules, and no theory yet joins it with gravity
In 2014 Carlo Rovelli and Hal Haggard suggested that matter may never reach that point
Squeezed to a limit it bounces back, the way a spring pressed all the way springs back hard
and that bounce turns the black hole into a white hole
Here it is all about time, because near a black hole time runs very slowly
For the matter inside, the bounce takes a second, but for anyone outside it can take billions of years, so today's black holes haven't turned white yet

c.at: और यहीं एक बड़ा Indian नाम
c.text: And here comes a big Indian name, Abhay Ashtekar, one of the founders of loop quantum gravity
In 2018, with Javier Olmedo and Parampreet Singh, he showed that in this theory the infinite-density point at the centre disappears
and a bridge forms there instead, joining the black hole to its opposite, a white hole

c.text: If black holes really become white holes, the change comes first in the smallest ones, because with less mass their bounce comes sooner
Some scientists think many tiny black holes formed just after the Big Bang and, over billions of years, became white holes
and their leftover pieces may still be drifting through space
Each piece is smaller than an atom and weighs like a small grain of sand; they neither shine nor collide with anything
We know them only by gravity, just like dark matter, which holds galaxies together but can't be seen
so Carlo Rovelli and colleagues suggested part of dark matter could be such white holes
This is only an idea for now, but there is a theory even bigger
In the Big Bang all matter and energy came out of one place and nothing went in; a white hole does exactly this, so some physicists think our Big Bang was like a giant white hole

c.text: So what are white holes? The last stage of black holes, the Big Bang's twin, or just maths that nature never lets happen?
Science hasn't decided yet, but whenever a blast without a star appears in space, scientists ask that same 2006 question again
